water-hydrogen-bonding-s1.title: Four liquids compared
water-hydrogen-bonding-s1.text: A class looked up two properties of four liquids at standard pressure. Water and ethanol molecules can form hydrogen bonds with each other; acetone molecules are polar but cannot; hexane molecules are nonpolar.

table.caption: Specific heat and heat of vaporization of four liquids
rows: Yes, up to four per molecule

water-hydrogen-bonding-s2.title: Warming two liquids
water-hydrogen-bonding-s2.text: A student placed 100 g of water in one beaker and 100 g of ethanol in an identical beaker, both starting at 20 °C. Each beaker sat on an identical hot plate set to deliver heat at the same rate, and the student recorded the temperature every minute.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Liquids whose molecules form more hydrogen bonds need more energy per gram to vaporize.
Liquids made of larger and heavier molecules need more energy per gram to turn into vapor.
Polar liquids that lack hydrogen bonds between molecules vaporize more easily than hexane.
A liquid's specific heat does not depend on how its molecules attract each other.

why.correct: Heat of vaporization falls in the same order as hydrogen bonding: water (most), then ethanol, then the two liquids with none.
options: Water, with the most hydrogen bonds per molecule, needs the most energy, and ethanol, with fewer, needs less: the pattern the data show.
Hexane has the largest molecules of the four and the lowest heat of vaporization, so size does not explain the pattern.
Acetone needs 539 J/g against hexane's 335 J/g, so acetone takes more energy to vaporize, not less.
Water, with the strongest attraction between molecules, has by far the highest specific heat, so the two are linked.

items.q: Using the table, how much energy, in kilojoules, is needed to evaporate 5.0 g of sweat? Treat sweat as pure water.

why.correct: Energy = mass × heat of vaporization = 5.0 g × 2,260 J/g = 11,300 J, which is 11.3 kJ (divide joules by 1,000).

items.q: Sweat cools the skin as it evaporates. Based on the table, why would water cool the skin better than the same mass of ethanol?
options: Each gram of water that evaporates removes about 2.7 times as much heat as a gram of ethanol.
Each gram of water that evaporates removes less heat, so more grams of it evaporate over time.
Water warms faster than ethanol, so it reaches the temperature of the skin sooner.
Ethanol has the higher specific heat, so it stores the heat instead of carrying it away.

why.correct: Evaporative cooling depends on heat of vaporization, and water's (2,260 J/g) is about 2.7 times ethanol's (841 J/g).
options: 2,260 J/g divided by 841 J/g is about 2.7, so every gram of water that evaporates carries away far more heat.
Water removes more heat per gram, not less: its heat of vaporization is the highest in the table.
Water has the higher specific heat, so it warms more slowly than ethanol, not faster.
Ethanol's specific heat (2.44) is lower than water's (4.18), and specific heat is not what evaporative cooling depends on.

items.q: Which statements does the table support? Select all that apply.
options: Water has the highest specific heat of the four liquids.
Acetone has a higher heat of vaporization than hexane.
Hexane has the lowest specific heat of the four liquids.
Ethanol's heat of vaporization is more than half of water's.

why.correct: Read each claim against the numbers: two match the table and two do not.
options: 4.18 J/g·°C is the largest value in the specific heat column.
539 J/g is greater than 335 J/g, so acetone needs more energy to vaporize than hexane.
Acetone's 2.15 is lower than hexane's 2.26, so hexane is not the lowest.
841 is about 37% of 2,260, which is less than half.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results in the graph?
options: Both liquids warm at a steady rate, and ethanol warms about 1.7 times as fast as water.
Both liquids warm at a steady rate, and water warms about 1.7 times as fast as ethanol.
Ethanol warms quickly at first and then levels off, while water warms at a steady rate.
The two liquids warm at the same rate until the third minute, and then ethanol pulls ahead.

why.correct: Both lines are straight, and ethanol rises 4.1 °C per minute against water's 2.4 °C per minute, a ratio of about 1.7.
options: Straight lines mean steady rates; 4.1 divided by 2.4 is about 1.7, and ethanol's line is the steeper one.
This reverses the two liquids: water's line is the less steep one.
Ethanol's line stays straight over the five minutes; it does not level off.
The lines separate from the first minute, not the third.

items.q: What is the rate at which the water's temperature rises over the five minutes?

why.correct: Rate = change in temperature ÷ time = (32.0 °C − 20.0 °C) ÷ 5 min = 2.4 °C per minute.

items.q: Which reasoning best explains why the water warms more slowly than the ethanol?
options: Some of the added energy breaks the many hydrogen bonds between water molecules instead of speeding them up.
Water molecules are heavier than ethanol molecules, so each one needs more added energy before it can move any faster.
Water absorbs less of the heat from the hot plate because liquid water is a good insulator.
Ethanol molecules form more hydrogen bonds, and forming them releases extra heat into the ethanol.

why.correct: With the same heat going in, the liquid that spends more energy breaking attractions between molecules shows a smaller rise in temperature.
options: Breaking water's many hydrogen bonds uses part of the energy, so less of it raises the temperature.
A water molecule (18 units of mass) is lighter than an ethanol molecule (46), so mass cannot explain it.
Both beakers received heat at the same rate; the difference is in what the energy does once absorbed.
Ethanol has one O–H group per molecule and forms fewer hydrogen bonds than water, not more.

items.q: Which variables had to be held the same for this comparison to be valid?
options: The mass of each liquid and the rate at which heat was supplied to it
The final temperature each liquid reached after five minutes
The rate at which the temperature of each liquid went up
The kind of liquid placed in each of the two beakers

why.correct: To blame the difference on the liquid, everything else that affects warming, such as mass and heating rate, must be the same.
options: A larger mass or a hotter plate would change the warming rate by itself, so both are controlled.
The final temperature is a result the student measured, so it is part of the dependent variable.
The warming rate is what the experiment measures; it is the dependent variable.
The kind of liquid is the independent variable: it is the one thing deliberately changed.

items.q: Why is a water molecule polar?
options: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer, so it is partly negative and the hydrogens are partly positive.
Hydrogen pulls the shared electrons closer, so the hydrogens are partly negative and the oxygen partly positive.
One side of the molecule carries a full positive charge and the other side a full negative charge.
Oxygen gives one electron to each hydrogen, so the molecule is made of ions held by ionic bonds.

why.correct: Unequal sharing of electrons gives water partial charges at its two ends.
options: Oxygen attracts electrons more strongly than hydrogen, which leaves partial charges on the two ends.
This reverses the pull: oxygen, not hydrogen, attracts the shared electrons more strongly.
The charges are partial, not full; water is a neutral molecule, not a pair of ions.
The electrons are shared in covalent bonds, not given away, so no ions form.

items.q: In liquid water, a hydrogen bond forms between which two atoms?
options: The partly positive hydrogen of one molecule and the partly negative oxygen of another
The two hydrogen atoms that belong to one water molecule
The oxygen atom and a hydrogen atom within the same water molecule
The partly negative oxygen atoms of two neighboring water molecules

why.correct: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, from a partly positive hydrogen to a partly negative oxygen.
options: Opposite partial charges on neighboring molecules attract: that attraction is the hydrogen bond.
The two hydrogens of one molecule both carry partial positive charges, so they repel rather than attract.
Oxygen and hydrogen in the same molecule share electrons in a covalent bond, which is a different and stronger bond.
Two partly negative oxygens repel each other.

items.q: Water climbs higher in a narrow glass tube than in a wide one. Which explanation fits best?
options: Water adheres to the glass walls, and cohesion pulls the rest of the column up behind it.
Water's high specific heat keeps the column at a steady temperature, so it can rise.
Hydrogen bonds form between the water and the air above it, lifting the surface up.
Evaporation from the top of the column cools the water, which makes it rise higher.

why.correct: In a narrow tube a larger share of the water touches the wall, so adhesion lifts it and cohesion drags the column along.
options: Adhesion to the polar glass pulls water up the walls, and cohesion keeps the column together as it rises.
Specific heat is about how temperature changes, not about water moving up a tube.
The gases in air are not the partly charged atoms a hydrogen bond needs.
Cooling makes the water denser; it does not lift water up a glass tube.

items.q: A student adds a drop of dish soap, which gets between water molecules at the surface and disrupts their hydrogen bonds, to a dish of water. Predict the change in each variable.

variables.name: Surface tension of the water
variables.why: With fewer hydrogen bonds at the surface, cohesion there is weaker, so the surface is easier to break.

variables.name: Number of paper clips the surface can float
variables.why: A weaker surface skin supports less weight, so fewer paper clips float before the surface breaks.

variables.name: Number of atoms in each water molecule
variables.why: Soap changes the attractions between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside each one, so every molecule still has three atoms.

why.correct: Surface tension comes from cohesion, which comes from hydrogen bonds; disrupting them weakens the surface without changing the molecules themselves.

items.q: Put the steps of cooling by sweating in order.
options: Heat from the skin makes the water molecules in sweat move faster.
The fastest molecules at the surface break all of their hydrogen bonds.
Those molecules escape as vapor, carrying their energy with them.
The molecules left behind move more slowly on average, so the sweat is cooler.
The cooler sweat takes more heat from the skin, and the cycle repeats.

why.correct: Evaporation removes the most energetic molecules, so the average energy, and so the temperature, of what is left goes down.

items.q: Which of these depends on hydrogen bonds between water molecules? Select all that apply.
options: The surface tension that lets a water strider stand on a pond
The bent shape of a single water molecule
The mass of a single water molecule
The bond between the oxygen and a hydrogen in one molecule

why.correct: Only properties that involve several molecules attracting each other depend on hydrogen bonds.
options: Surface tension comes from cohesion, the hydrogen bonds between molecules at the surface.
The shape belongs to one molecule and comes from how its electrons are arranged, not from its neighbors.
Mass comes from the atoms in the molecule, which hydrogen bonds do not change.
That is a covalent bond inside the molecule, not a hydrogen bond between molecules.

items.q: Over a summer day the air above a large lake warms by 12 °C, but the lake's surface water warms by less than 2 °C. Which reasoning best explains the difference?
options: Water's high specific heat means each gram must absorb a lot of energy to warm by one degree.
Water's low specific heat means the lake absorbs very little of the sun's energy during the day.
Hydrogen bonds stop heat from entering the water, so the sun's energy barely warms the lake.
Warm water evaporates more slowly than cool water, so the lake keeps its heat at the surface.

why.correct: Much of the energy the lake absorbs goes into breaking hydrogen bonds, so water's temperature rises far less than the air's for the same energy input.
options: About 4.18 J warms one gram of water by just one degree, so a whole lake absorbs a great deal of energy with little change in temperature.
Water's specific heat is high, not low, and the lake does absorb energy; its temperature simply rises slowly.
Energy does enter the water; breaking hydrogen bonds uses much of it, which slows the temperature rise.
Warm water evaporates faster, not more slowly, and evaporation removes heat from the surface rather than keeping it.
